transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-02 15:00 UTC
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Raj (Redwood SE), Tom (Nimbus Eng Manager), Sara (Nimbus Head of ML), Diego (Nimbus Infra)

Summary (auto): Migration demo focusing on parity mapping and migration plan from OpenAI/Anthropic/Together to Redwood. Action items captured.

Topics: parity mapping, API differences, embeddings mapping, streaming & function-calling, Dedicated vs Hosted vs Private, Optimize recommendations (batching/quantization/caching), security & compliance (SOC2, SSO, KMS)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on this account, and Raj our solutions engineer is on to do the deep-dive. Tom, Sara, Diego, thanks for coming. Quick agenda — parity mapping, console walkthrough, Optimize suggestions, and next steps.
[00:18] Tom: Yeah thanks, we have, uh, about 45 minutes. We want to understand how close Redwood is to the APIs we use today — we currently have a mix of OpenAI and Together endpoints for generation and Anthropic for some safety models. Primary ask: minimal code changes and predictable latency/cost.
[00:35] Raj: Great, we'll start with the API parity. At a high level Redwood provides the same primitives — chat-style messages, system/user/assistant roles, completions parameters like temperature, top_p, max_tokens, and stop sequences. Differences to note: Redwood's SDK normalizes role names and has a slightly different streaming chunk envelope; we provide compatibility layers and example mappers.
[00:50] Raj: Example: OpenAI uses messages array with role and content, Anthropic uses a single prompt with A/B system. Together has its own fields. We showed a code snippet mapping OpenAI/Anthropic/Together messages into Redwood's chat format — it's mostly mechanical: map role names and keep system messages as-is.
[01:20] Sara: What about temperature and top_p behaviors? We noticed variance across the providers.
[01:26] Raj: Good question. Temperature and top_p semantics are the same, but model-specific defaults differ. In the parity doc we'll include recommended starting values per model, and Redwood Optimize will suggest per-workload tuning (it can propose temperature/top_p/beam settings from historic evals).
[01:42] Diego: Streaming — how different is the streaming protocol? We stream today from OpenAI and rely on token-level latencies.
[01:48] Raj: Redwood supports SSE and gRPC streaming. The chunk payload is similar but note: we include token metadata for KV cache hints to support prefix caching. If you have code that consumes OpenAI SSE, the mapping is 1:1 for message chunks; we'll share an adapter example.
[02:15] Maya: Quick demo — I'll share the console and show model selection and rollout.
[02:22] [screen share noise]
[02:35] Maya: Here's the Models tab — curated open models and Redwood-verified performance profiles. You can pin versions, create rollouts (canary/A-B), and set fallback model variants if capacity is low.
[02:50] Tom: Nice. How does the rollback work? Say a model degrades after a rollout.
[02:55] Raj: You can configure automatic fallback policies by latency or quality SLOs; if the canary crosses a threshold the orchestrator will route to the previous stable variant automatically.
[03:10] Sara: Embeddings — we use text-embedding-3-small and some proprietary variants. How do we map?
[03:17] Raj: Redwood offers several embedding models; the parity mapping doc lists nearest equivalents and notes any vector-dim differences. For example, OpenAI text-embedding-3-small -> Redwood-embed-small (dim 1536) we recommend reindexing if dims differ, but we also support on-the-fly projection for a short-term compatibility layer.
[03:40] Diego: Any performance differences for embeddings? We use high-QPS for search.
[03:45] Raj: For high QPS we recommend Dedicated pools. Optimize can advise batching windows and caching hot vectors. For embeddings we recommend vectorize-in-batches with async ingestion; we'll show a sample harness.
[04:05] Tom: Function calling is big for us — we have a number of structured tool calls today. How does Redwood map the OpenAI function-calling spec?
[04:12] Raj: Redwood supports function/tool-calling and structured outputs. The mapping is straightforward: OpenAI functions -> Redwood tools. The difference is we attach tool metadata for routing (e.g., which runtime executes the tool) and optional RBAC gating for sensitive tools. We'll share examples converting OpenAI-style function declarations to Redwood tool schema and show sample handler signatures.
[04:35] [05:00] Speaker 1 (Sara): Any gotchas around stop sequences? We rely on them for some extraction tasks.
[05:07] Raj: Redwood supports stop sequences and structured completions; note that some models behave differently with overlapping stops — Optimize will include tests to catch regressions. We recommend adding unit tests around prompt/eval sets during migration.
[05:25] Maya: Now onto costs — we walked through token accounting, batching and caching levers.
[05:32] Raj: Right, cost differences are a combination of model compute and your usage pattern. Optimize can propose batching configurations — e.g., 20–60ms batching windows for chat-heavy routes can drastically reduce per-token cost with minimal p95 latency impact. Also KV/prefix caching can save cost for long documents.
[05:55] Tom: Can Optimize suggest quantization profiles? We are considering 4-bit quant models to save $$$.
[06:02] Raj: Yes, Optimize has suggested quantization profiles per model type and workload. It will recommend 4-bit/8-bit profiles and predict quality delta; you can run A/B tests via the rollout system.
[06:18] Diego: Security — we need SOC2, SSO, audit logs, and KMS.
[06:24] Maya: Redwood is SOC 2 Type II. We provide SSO/SAML, OIDC, RBAC, audit logs, and for Private/Dedicated deployments we support customer-managed KMS and HSM integrations. For Hosted we offer envelope encryption with customer keys (bring-your-own-key). We'll attach the security whitepaper.
[06:46] Sara: Data residency — can we keep data in EU and have logs off by default?
[06:52] Raj: Yes, region pinning is available and you can set retention policies per-project. For strict requirements our Private deployment with on-prem options is the recommended path.
[07:05] Tom: Networking — VPC peering?
[07:08] Diego: (chiming) yes, we need to know exact ports and cert requirements.
[07:12] Raj: We support VPC peering and private link depending on cloud provider; I'll put Diego in touch with our infra onboarding doc which lists ports, CIDR ranges, and certificate expectations.
[07:28] Maya: Demo — simple migration code example (mapping snippet).
[07:34] Raj: (reads code) On OpenAI you'd call openai.chat.completions.create({messages, temperature}), on Redwood you'd call redwood.chat.create({messages, temp}) — our SDK includes a small shim so you can keep existing function names while swapping endpoints. We'll push a repo with examples for OpenAI, Anthropic and Together mappings.
[08:10] Sara: How are rate limits handled? We have bursty traffic.
[08:15] Raj: Hosted has quotas and rate limits; Dedicated provides reserved pools with autoscaling and burst capacity. You can also configure backpressure and graceful queuing.
[08:28] Tom: SLA?
[08:30] Maya: Dedicated gets an SLA-backed uptime and latency target; Hosted has standard availability guarantees and enterprise add-on SLAs. We'll include the SLA summary in the next email.
[08:40] Diego: Can you run a sample P95 latency benchmark for our prompt set? We care about p95 under 400ms for short chat requests.
[08:46] Raj: Yes — we'll run the benchmark on Dedicated and Hosted so you can compare. We'll focus on real prompt sampling and the same concurrency pattern.
[09:00] [09:30] Speaker 2 (Tom): Ok let's talk about regressions — we want quality validation post-migration.
[09:36] Raj: Redwood has an evals pipeline in Optimize where you can define prompt sets and expected outputs, run A/B comparisons between upstream model and target model, and set alerts for quality regressions. You can also tie rollouts to eval pass rates.
[09:55] Sara: Do you support multi-model routing? We sometimes route to Anthropic for safety checks.
[10:02] Raj: Yes, smart routing can route by policy — for example route to Anthropic for safety checks, otherwise route to Redwood model. In Dedicated you can pin variants and set fallback chains.
[10:16] Maya: We'll also provide a parity spreadsheet — column for OpenAI/Anthropic/Together field and Redwood equivalent plus code snippet.
[10:29] Tom: Great. About cost modelling — can you show us cost per 1M tokens for the model family?
[10:35] Raj: We gave rough figures in the deck; final pricing will depend on Dedicated commit or Hosted usage. We'll send a modeled comparison based on your monthly qps after you share sample traffic.
[10:48] Sara: Any known incompatibilities?
[10:51] Raj: Few edge cases: some Together models have slightly different tokenization leading to token count variance; some Anthropic system prompt behaviors differ — those are mapped in parity doc and we suggest small prompt adjustments and unit tests.
[11:10] Diego: Ops — how do we do key rotation and audit?
[11:13] Maya: Key rotation via KMS integration; audit logs are available in Console and exportable to your SIEM. We'll include sample retention configs.
[11:26] Raj: For the POC we'd recommend a 3-week pilot: week 1 migration and smoke tests, week 2 benchmark and cost tuning, week 3 rollout test and evals.
[11:40] Tom: That timeline looks fine.
[11:44] Maya: Ok quick recap and next steps.
[11:46] Maya: 1) We send parity mapping doc + example repo. 2) Raj runs benchmark and shares results. 3) Nimbus shares prompt sets, Diego checks networking. 4) We target pilot week starting 2025-10-13.
[12:05] Sara: Sounds good. Thanks.
[12:09] Diego: Thanks all.
[12:12] Maya: We'll follow up with the docs and calendar invites. Bye.
[12:18] End of recording.
